adjudication.rationale: The ratchet is real; the reviewer's 'caller-supplied clock' framing is not. `DegradedWindow::record_read` is `fetch_max(now)` (admission_enforcer/degraded_window.rs:49-51) and `exhausted` computes `now.saturating_sub(last)` (:65-69), so the base is monotone by design. `now` is the serving path's own wall clock — `now_unix()` read once per request in app.rs:949 and threaded through `handle` — not anything a caller supplies, so there is no remote reachability and the reviewer's 'if any caller ever derives now from something an attacker influences' is not a live path. What survives is the operational one: one forward step of T seconds (NTP step, VM resume, a wall-vs-monotonic mix-up) sets the base T into the future, `now - last` is then negative, never `> P + skew`, and the window reads as OPEN for the T seconds the real clock takes to catch up — during a store outage, which is when revocations cannot propagate. There is no plausibility clamp, no reset, and `DegradedWindow` exposes no projection, so nothing can observe or report it. The same forward step also expires assertions, which bounds the damage but does not remove it.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Measure the outage in `DegradedWindow` from a monotonic instant rather than from the wall clock: keep the last successful read as an `Instant`-derived offset so a wall-clock step cannot move the base, and add a projection so the posture/health line can report how long the authority has been unreachable. The wall clock stays where it belongs, on assertion and record freshness.

adjudication.rationale: True at main. `admission_key` formats `admission_id` verbatim into the shared-store key (admission_source/mod.rs:111-113) with the doc justifying the verbatim form on operator-legibility grounds — a good argument for not digesting it and none at all for not bounding it. The id arrives inside the request evidence block as `AdmissionBinding::admission_id`, a plain `String` (admission.rs:146), and `HttpRequestEvidenceBlock::validate` bounds the ASSERTION (`MAX_ADMISSION_ASSERTION_LEN`, block.rs:493-500) and imposes no length, charset or content rule on the binding beside it. `decide` then issues a GET on it per request (admission_enforcer/mod.rs:118) before anything is verified about it. adjudication.rationale: Same root cause as R11-159: `actor_id` is a `pub Option<String>` on a publicly mintable `pub struct` (mcp-re-proxy/src/audit_record/mod.rs:66-78, lib.rs:327), and the admission ceiling keys on its mere inhabitation at audit_sink/mod.rs:130. The fix is the same one — a resolution witness in place of the bare `Option<String>`, with the record's representation private to `crate::audit_record` — and grouping them apart would produce two PRs editing the same four lines. The second half of the detail (that `StderrAuditSink` and `AuditSink::record` are `pub`, so a caller can reach the queue without the funnel) is likewise R11-159's, and the delivery entry point narrows with the same change.

title: The attribution ceiling classifies on a `pub` field any caller can set

adjudication.rationale: The same proposition as R11-161, restated: `AuditSubject::request` does not bind the Core event to the request half, and `AuditSubject::response(AuditEvent::request_accepted())` is symmetrically constructible (mcp-re-proxy/src/audit_record/mod.rs:100-110). One half-typed pair of constructors closes both. Nothing in this row's mechanism differs; its `pub` fields observation is R11-159's.

title: `AuditSubject::request` does not bind the Core event to the request half

adjudication.rationale: True at main with the file moved: the funnel is now `record_to` at mcp-re-proxy/src/audit_record/mod.rs:183-198, and it calls `sink.record(&AuditRecord { .. })` at :191 with no `catch_unwind`, no timeout and no bulkhead. A workspace grep confirms `record_to` is the sole production emission funnel (five call sites: receipt/audit_event.rs:47 and :94, pre_admission/mod.rs:136, reply_assembly/accepted.rs:63, reply_assembly/notification.rs:78) and that no production code calls `AuditSink::record` anywhere else. The trait's two MUSTs at audit_sink/mod.rs:37-45 are correctly phrased as implementor obligations, and mod.rs:55-62 is explicit that the hand-off discharges them for `StderrAuditSink` only — so nothing OVERCLAIMS and this is not `claim-only`. What is true is that `AuditSink` is `pub`, `AuditRecord` is `pub`, and `HttpProfileProxy::with_audit_sink` is `pub`, so an embedder's `record` runs inside the request future on the preflight rejection path, and its panic kills the connection task. Revised medium to low: the blocking half cannot be mechanically contained behind a synchronous trait seam, and reaching it requires an embedder's own sink.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In the funnel `record_to` (`mcp-re-proxy/src/audit_record`), wrap the single `sink.record(..)` call in `std::panic::catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(..))` so a third-party sink's panic degrades to one lost record rather than a killed connection task — the funnel is the one place that costs nothing and the only place that covers every emitter. The blocking half is not containable synchronously; say so on the trait doc at audit_sink/mod.rs:37-45 (the obligation is the implementor's, and the funnel contains the panic but not the latency) rather than leaving a reader to infer that `record_to` holds both.

title: No panic or timeout barrier around `sink.record` in the one funnel

notes: Undecided inside its packet; needs crate::authorization audit-fields renderer — whether it can ever emit a Core mcp-re.* verification token

adjudication.rationale: The neighbouring renderer the reviewer needed disproves the generality worry. `AuditSubject::audit_fields` (mcp-re-proxy/src/audit_record.rs:118-123) passes ONLY the authorization facet to the renderer and never hands it the Core `AuditEvent`, and `AuthorizationFacet::audit_fields` (mcp-re-proxy/src/authorization/audit/fields.rs:36-61) emits only `authz*` keys whose sole token source is `PolicyError::wire_code()` (mcp-re-policy/src/error.rs:107), every member of which is an `mcp-re.authorization_*` string (error.rs:17-57). So 'no Core verification token in the authorization coordinate' is structural, not sampled, and the weak negative at audit_record.rs:207 is not load-bearing — the positive assertion at :203-206 already excludes the empty-string regression the finding names.

adjudication.rationale: `the_epoch_domain_names_the_current_definition` is `assert_eq!(EPOCH_DOMAIN, b"mcp-re/tls-auth-epoch/v2")` (`auth_epoch.rs:338-341`) — a constant compared against a literal copy of itself, which says nothing about whether the domain enters the digest. Deleting `hasher.update((EPOCH_DOMAIN.len() as u64).to_be_bytes())` and `hasher.update(EPOCH_DOMAIN)` (:100-101) leaves it green, and leaves every other epoch control green too, because they all compare epochs against other epochs (:285-333, :344-407) — a uniformly weaker digest is invisible to all of them. The same holds for the length delimiters the doc calls load-bearing (:69-73): nothing pins that moving a byte between the count prefix and an anchor changes the value. The test is registered as evidence for `proxy.tls_listener_state` (`verification/policy/verification.toml:549`), so the unit's fingerprint carries an assertion about a string's spelling in place of one about the function's definition. No attacker story — nothing else in the tree hashes raw anchor DER — so severity medium -> low.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In `mcp-re-proxy/src/tls_listener_state/auth_epoch.rs`, add a golden-vector control pinning `TlsAuthEpoch::compute` over a fixed anchor vector against a hard-coded 32-byte expected digest, so deleting the domain update, the length prefixes or the ordering moves a value the test names; register it in the unit's tested_symbols in place of, or beside, the spelling assertion.

adjudication.rationale: The branch is real and unmeasured. `unwrap_if_current` uses `stored.split_at_checked(tag.len())?` (`auth_epoch.rs:224-233`), so a stored value shorter than 32 bytes yields `None` and is treated as a mismatch — evicted by `get` (:245-257), already removed by `take` (:259-264). Every test in the file writes through `put` (:237-243), which always prefixes the full tag, so no control puts an untagged or short value into the inner cache; the branch is code-reading-only while THM-0103's statement asserts it outright ('a stored value too short to carry a tag is a mismatch'). The cost of measuring it is one test: `EpochBoundSessionStore::new` takes any `Arc<dyn StoresServerSessions>` (:188-193), so a pre-populated `ServerSessionMemoryCache` holding a short value is constructible inside this module. Severity stays low — the only producer of such a value is an inner store this type did not write.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In `mcp-re-proxy/src/tls_listener_state/auth_epoch.rs`, add a control that constructs an `EpochBoundSessionStore` over a `ServerSessionMemoryCache` pre-loaded with a value shorter than 32 bytes and asserts `get`/`take` return `None` and that `get` evicted it; register it in the unit's tested_symbols.

adjudication.rationale: The accounting gap exists but it is smaller than stated, and the reviewer's proposed fix is the one this registry has already ruled against. True: `TlsAuthEpoch::compute` is a SHA-256 (`auth_epoch.rs:87-110`), `unwrap_if_current` decides resumption by comparing those 32 bytes (:224-233), `ASM-0037`'s scope is `unit://http_profile.keyid_selector` and `boundary://boundary.crypto_primitives` (`verification/policy/assumptions.toml`), and `boundary.crypto_primitives` names only `mcp-re-core/src/crypto.rs` and `hash.rs` (`verification/policy/trust-boundaries.toml:51-59`) — `auth_epoch.rs` uses `sha2` directly, so it sits in neither. False, or at least overstated: the unit's headline consequence does not rest on the premise. Under ADR-MCPRE-062 model A the epoch is a construction-time constant, so what protects an anchor-set change is cache NON-CONTINUITY — a new anchor set is a new listener with a new empty store (`tls_listener_state/mod.rs:29-34`, `a_different_anchor_set_is_a_different_state_with_its_own_empty_cache` :303) — not digest inequality. And the anchors are operator-supplied, so the adversarial collision-resistance ASM-0037 states (an adversary free to choose BOTH strings) is not the property relied on. Widening ASM-0037's scope is precisely what the owner ruling quoted in `assumptions.toml` withdrew: 'a scope is not a restatement, and a premise a consumer does not actually rely on is not made true by naming that consumer.' Severity medium -> low.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In `verification/policy/theorems.toml`, state in THM-0103's scope that the store's tag comparison is byte equality and that digest INEQUALITY for the anchor sets it names is witnessed by the controls rather than assumed, with model A's cache non-continuity named as what carries the anchor-change consequence. Do not widen ASM-0037.

But of the two possible answers to a branch proved unreachable, the one written is `i64::MAX` — which makes `now.saturating_sub(iat) > max_decision_age.saturating_add(skew)` (mcp-re-http-profile/src/pdp_decision/verify.rs:130) unable to fire at all, i.e. the deployment silently accepts decisions of ANY age while its ON line at capability.rs:60-69 still prints a finite number. That is a fail-open default guarding an invariant owned elsewhere, and the refusing alternative is already in hand: `evaluator()` returns `Result<_, String>` and refuses startup on the empty-issuer case eight lines above (:51-59), so declining the conversion costs nothing structurally. No attacker story while the Layer-A narrowing holds; the finding is that the narrowing's owner is the only thing keeping it true, and the fallback hides the day it stops being.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In `mcp-re-proxy/src/authorization/capability.rs`, replace `.unwrap_or(i64::MAX)` at :81-82 with a refusing conversion — `i64::try_from(..).map_err(|_| format!("--authz-max-decision-age-secs {} does not fit the verifier's staleness bound", ...))?` — so the impossible branch fails startup instead of selecting the widest accepting value, and rewrite the :79-80 comment to state the invariant it now merely explains rather than relies on. The deeper fix, typing `PdpDecisionFreshness::max_decision_age` so 'no bound' is unrepresentable, crosses into mcp-re-http-profile and is not the smallest correct change.

adjudication.rationale: Reachable, and the stage ordering the finding asked for is what makes it so. `authorization_stage` is the LAST stage of `admit_request` (pre_admission/mod.rs:111-113), and `commit_to_answering` runs after it (http_profile_serve/mod.rs:466-478). Every refusal `commit_to_answering` raises is `Refusal::before_admission` with a Core cause — replay admission 409 (answering_commitment.rs:58), `DelegatedSigningUnavailable` 503 (:82-85), `ContinuationBindingFailed` 409 (:114), `ReplayCacheUnavailable` 503 (:127) — so posture is `BeforeAdmission`, `receipt::refuse` routes it to `rejection` (receipt/mod.rs:144), and `rejection` composes `cause.authorization_facet()` (receipt/audit_event.rs:56), which maps EVERY Core arm to `Refused(BeforePolicy)` (refusal/cause.rs:115-122) and renders `authz=refused-before-policy` (authorization/audit/fields.rs:51-53). Concrete path: a deployment with an authorization policy that PERMITS the action; the request then replays a nonce (or the delegated key snapshot is unavailable); the emitted record says `event=mcp-re.request.rejected reason=mcp-re.replay_detected ... authz=refused-before-policy` for a request a policy in fact allowed. That is the positive misattribution authorization/audit.rs:141-143 says the two arms exist to prevent, in the exact 'operator sent to inspect a grant that was never consulted' direction, inverted. Note the facet is not `NotReached` — `Refused(BeforePolicy)` asserts no policy verdict was reached.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Carry the established `AuthorizationPosture` that `admit_request` already returns (`AdmittedRequest.authorized`, pre_admission/mod.rs:44-47) onto the `Exchange`, and have `HttpProfileProxy::refuse` compose the record's facet from `posture.audit_facet()` whenever a posture exists, falling back to `cause.authorization_facet()` only for refusals raised before the authorization stage ran. `BeforePolicy` then becomes claimable only where no policy ran, which is what the arm's doc asserts.

adjudication.rationale: The ordering is described accurately but evaluated in only one direction. Inside `attempt_reload`'s closure the rebuilt config is produced first (`crl_reload_worker/mod.rs:148-150`), the new index is then published (:151-153), and `config_snapshot::reload_once` swaps the config when the closure returns — so a rebuild failure publishes nothing and the stated failure-atomicity rule holds. The window the finding names is between :152 and the swap, a few instructions. The reviewer did not evaluate the alternative: publishing the index AFTER the swap would mean new handshakes use the NEW verifier (refusing a newly revoked serial) while established connections are still checked against the OLD index (admitting it) — the permissive direction, on exactly the connections the per-request half exists to reach. The current order publishes the TIGHTENING half first, so the only disagreement it can produce is the handshake verifier being stricter than the index for a serial an operator has just UN-revoked. That is the fail-closed choice, and with two independent atomics (`SharedClientRevocation` and `ServerConfigSnapshot`) a genuinely joint swap is not available without a single value carrying both halves. Severity low -> info.

adjudication.rationale: The out-of-packet question is answered in the finding's favour: `HttpInnerPool::prepare` takes a bounded owned in-flight permit (`try_acquire_owned`, refusing with `NotAdmitted` when the pool is full — mcp-re-proxy/src/http_inner/mod.rs:474-482) and, on a HalfOpen backend, also claims the breaker's single recovery-probe slot (mcp-re-proxy/src/http_inner/mod.rs:487-498). Both are moved into the not-yet-run transmit closure (:502-507), so they are held from `commit_to_dispatch`'s line 83 across `self.retention.reserve(..).await` (dispatch_commitment.rs:87) and `self.retention.commit(..).await` (:91). Neither await is a queue-and-go: `EvidenceRetention::reserve` and `commit_to_dispatch` each `submit(..).await` a durable job and wait for the writer's acknowledgement (mcp-re-proxy/src/transparency/durability.rs:198-204, 238-242), which retention.rs:71-75 states includes the fsync. Concrete reachable outcome, retention enabled: with store acknowledgement latency L, every in-flight inner permit is occupied for L longer than the backend round trip, so the pool saturates at concurrency C where C·(D+2L) exceeds the bound and `prepare` returns `NotAdmitted` — a 503 shed for requests the backend could have served, plus a HalfOpen backend whose one trial slot is pinned for 2L, delaying breaker recovery. The module doc's claim at dispatch_commitment.rs:66-72 is about LEAKING capacity and is true; it does not cover holding.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Keep the ordering, bound the wait: give `Retention::reserve` and `Retention::commit` an explicit deadline (they already fail closed on error, so a timeout is an existing refusal shape) so the inner permit's hold time has a ceiling that does not depend on store health. The larger fix — separating the capacity DECISION from capability ACQUISITION so the permit is taken at the crossing — changes what `prepare` means and should not be done as a bug fix.

title: `AuditDrain::Drained` claims records reached stderr, but the writer discards every write error

adjudication.rationale: True at main. `report_drops` has exactly two production call sites, both inside the writer loop (mcp-re-proxy/src/audit_sink/writer.rs:122 on the Flush arm and :133 on every other iteration), so the shutdown flush of the drop count happens only if the `Flush` message is actually delivered. `drain::flush` returns early with `OutcomeUnknown` when `queue.try_send(AuditMessage::Flush(ack))` fails (drain.rs:70-72), which is precisely the full-queue condition under which records were being dropped — so the process exits with a non-zero, never-reported `STDERR_AUDIT_DROPPED`. The `OutcomeUnknown` line does point the operator at the seq gaps (drain.rs:101-109), so this degrades detail rather than destroying the signal, and it also covers the dead-writer case that R11-171's channel-sizing fix does not. The `Drained`-with-no-writer early return at :65-68 is not part of this: an empty `OnceLock` means `offer` never ran, so the counter is zero.
adjudication.smallest_fix: On the `OutcomeUnknown` return in `drain::flush` (or once in `at_shutdown` before it speaks), report the outstanding drop count from the shutdown thread itself instead of depending on the queue being drained. `STDERR_AUDIT_DROPPED` and `report_drops` are already `pub(super)`/module-local in `audit_sink::writer`, which `audit_sink::drain` can see — it already imports `writes_have_failed` the same way — so no visibility widens: the drain calls the same formatter against `std::io::stderr().lock()`, and the swap-and-put-back already makes double reporting impossible.

title: Outstanding drops are never reported when the drain cannot deliver its Flush — the case where drops are most likely

notes: Undecided inside its packet; needs the composition root / shutdown owner (app.rs) — how `report` is derived

adjudication.rationale: `report` is not a free caller-chosen bool: it is derived from the installed-sink fact at mcp-re-proxy/src/app.rs:260 (`config.audit_sink == AuditSinkKind::Stderr`), which is the same input that selects `StderrAuditSink` — `AuditSinkKind::Stderr -> AuditState::Stderr` (config_state/evidence.rs:86-87) -> `Arc::new(StderrAuditSink)` (serving_capabilities.rs:170-174). The only other value installs `NoAuditSink` and passes `report = false`. The pairing the finding worries about ('a custom AuditSink with report = true') has no producer through `app::run`. The `STDERR_AUDIT_WRITER == None -> Drained` arm (drain.rs:62-65) is then vacuously true for zero records, which is what `Drained` means.

title: `flush` reports a clean drain for a deployment whose writer was never started

adjudication.rationale: The accounting asymmetry is real and has a sharper consequence than the finding states. `STDERR_AUDIT_QUEUED` is incremented only by `offer`'s reservation (audit_sink/mod.rs:177) and decremented only on the writer's `Line` arm (writer.rs:118); `drain::flush` sends `AuditMessage::Flush` with a bare `try_send` and takes no slot (drain.rs:69-72). The channel is `sync_channel(STDERR_AUDIT_QUEUE_DEPTH)` (writer.rs:78-79) and the attributed ceiling IS `STDERR_AUDIT_QUEUE_DEPTH` (mod.rs:138), so at full legitimate line occupancy the channel has no room for the control message: the Flush cannot be enqueued, `flush` returns `OutcomeUnknown` IMMEDIATELY, and the 2s bound at drain.rs:23 is never used in exactly the case it was designed for — a writer that is merely behind and would have caught up. Overturning the reviewer's framing slightly: `OutcomeUnknown` for a genuinely stalled writer is correct; what is wrong is that a healthy backlogged one gets the same answer without the wait.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Give the control message a slot the line ceiling cannot take, in the writer that owns the channel: size it `sync_channel(STDERR_AUDIT_QUEUE_DEPTH + 1)` at `mcp-re-proxy/src/audit_sink/writer.rs:78-79`, so the reservation ceiling and the channel capacity stop being the same number and a `Flush` is always enqueueable while the writer lives. Say in the same place that `STDERR_AUDIT_QUEUED` counts LINES only, and in drain.rs that a `Flush` the disconnected channel refuses is the dead-writer case rather than the full-queue one.

adjudication.rationale: True at main, with the mechanism as described: `EvidenceRetention::complete` (durability.rs:331-350) takes `committed: &DispatchCommitted` plus an independent `request`, serializes `RetainedHopRecord::of(request, response)` for the hop bytes, and clears the marker named by `committed.digest()` — nothing compares the two. `DispatchCommitted` (dispatch_committed.rs:48-55) holds only a digest, a shared permit and the completion flag, so which exchange the hop must describe is carried by whatever the caller passes, not by the value. Applying the project's operational test: there is no check to delete, and a hop discharging a crossing it does not describe is constructible by any caller — the store's own test does the pairing by convention, holding `(request, committed)` tuples in a Vec (durability.rs:818-839). No live defect: the one production call site passes the same `&HttpRequest` borrow to both steps (dispatch_commitment.rs:87 `reserve(ex.http_req)` and reply_assembly/accepted.rs:100-113 `complete(retention_owed, request=ex.http_req, ...)`), and `with_evidence_retention` is a consuming builder so the store cannot change mid-exchange (http_profile_serve/mod.rs:246-251). adjudication.smallest_fix: Give `DispatchCommitted` the retained request it committed to — it already holds the digest of exactly those bytes — and reduce `EvidenceRetention::complete` to `complete(&self, committed: &DispatchCommitted, response: &HttpResponse)`. The serialized `RetainedRequest` is already computed in `reserve` (durability.rs:266-269), so carrying it forward costs one move and removes the parameter through which a mismatched pairing enters. A recompute-and-compare inside `complete` is the weaker alternative: it is a check, and a check is what R-SEAL says can be deleted.

title: `EvidenceRetention::retain` mints a hop with no execution boundary and no marker, restricted by documentation only

notes: Undecided inside its packet; needs proxy.replay_admission_gate and the composition root: whether retention can be configured without a refusing replay tier, and what the tier's window is. The packet contains no way to answer either.

adjudication.rationale: The premise is structural, just not at the store. `AsyncReplayTier` is a mandatory (non-`Option`) argument to `HttpProfileProxy::new_delegated` (http_profile_serve/mod.rs:265-274) and `replay_admission_stage` is an unconditional pipeline stage (answering_commitment.rs:157, reached from mod.rs:477), so retention cannot be enabled on a proxy that has no refusing replay tier — only its DURABILITY CLASS varies. The bounded-window objection does not bite either: the replay key's TTL is the signature's own `verified.expires()` (http_profile_dispatch.rs:165), and the verifier refuses a signature past `expires + skew` (verify/floor/params.rs:73-83) with the window itself bounded by `policy.max_signature_validity()` (:94) — so a byte-identical request outside the replay window fails verification rather than being admitted a second time. The 'requests differing only in uncovered headers collide' objection fails because `covered_headers` keeps `signature`/`signature-input` unconditionally (covered_set.rs:45-47), putting the nonce and the signature bytes in the digest input.

title: The marker's call identity depends on a replay tier this owner neither requires nor checks

adjudication.rationale: The window is real and the residue is harmless; what is wrong is a stated property. `reserve` awaits the marker publication (durability.rs:273-277) and constructs the rescind-bearing value only afterwards (durability.rs:278-283), so a future cancelled at that await leaves a published `<digest>.reserved` with no value whose `Drop` would withdraw it. The admission permit is correctly released (the local `permit` binding drops), so the only cost is disk debt — and a reserved-stage marker is honest debt by construction: it asserts no execution and is enumerable through `stale_reservations` (durability.rs:369-380). The claim that is false is `ReservedBeforeDispatch`'s: 'a refusal, an early return, a panic and a cancelled request future all drop, and dropping is the rescind' (reserved_before_dispatch.rs:42-44) — a cancelled request future does not drop a value that does not exist yet. `stale_reservations`' own doc enumerates two causes for a stale marker (a full queue, a dead process) and this is a third.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Narrow the two docs to what holds: `ReservedBeforeDispatch` rescinds for every exit AFTER it exists, and a cancellation inside `reserve` is the third source of stale reserved-stage debt `stale_reservations` enumerates. If the property is wanted rather than the honest statement, the code fix is small too — take the rescind responsibility before the await (a guard holding the marker path and a sender clone, whose `Drop` queues a `Rescind`, upgraded into `ReservedBeforeDispatch` once the ack returns); the rescind is already NotFound-tolerant (durable_writer.rs:103-110), so an unpublished marker costs nothing.

title: A request future cancelled inside `reserve` leaves a marker with nothing alive to rescind it

adjudication.rationale: Spending the completion before the write is attempted is load-bearing, not an oversight. `complete` takes it first (durability.rs:337-339) because the queue-capacity argument counts ONE job per permit: a completion that could be re-attempted would put a second job behind the same permit, which is exactly the post-execution capacity refusal the whole permit scheme exists to prevent — stated at dispatch_committed.rs:38-46 and asserted by `a_reservation_is_worth_exactly_one_completion` (durability.rs:949-992). The diagnostic conflation the finding describes is also unreachable on the serving path: `complete` is called at most once per exchange, from one of two mutually exclusive terminals (http_profile_serve/mod.rs:505-517 -> reply_assembly/accepted.rs:111-114), so `AlreadyCompleted` never reaches the 500 mapping at all. Nothing claims a retryable completion, so there is no claim to narrow either.

title: `complete` spends the single completion before the write is attempted

adjudication.rationale: Same root cause: marker identity is the request digest and the uniqueness premise is attributed to the replay tier. Disproved the same way — the tier is a mandatory constructor argument with an unconditional pipeline stage, the replay window is the signature's own `expires` (which the verifier enforces), and the digest input contains the `Signature`/`Signature-Input` headers verbatim.

title: Marker identity is the request digest with nothing requiring the replay tier that makes it unique; a colliding exchange can erase a committed crossing

notes: Undecided inside its packet; needs app.rs / startup_plan — whether the store is dropped on a normal shutdown path at all, or whether the process simply exits. That decides whether this is latent or live.

adjudication.rationale: The mechanism is exactly as described — `reserve` clones the `SyncSender` into every reservation (durability.rs:208, held at reserved_before_dispatch.rs:58), so `write_loop`'s `jobs.recv()` (durable_writer.rs:41) cannot return `Err` while one is alive and `Drop`'s `writer.join()` (durability.rs:85-87) would block — but the composition root the finding asked about makes the state unreachable. `MaterializedRuntime` drains FIRST: `fleet.shutdown_and_join()` returns only after every per-core worker thread has exited (async_fleet/mod.rs:149-160), and a worker exiting drops its per-core tokio runtime and with it every in-flight request future, hence every `ReservedBeforeDispatch` it held (async_fleet/mod.rs:141-146). The proxy — and the `Arc<EvidenceRetention>` inside its `Retention` — is reclaimed only in phase 3 (materialized_runtime.rs:11-16, 184-192). `DispatchCommitted` holds no sender at all (dispatch_committed.rs:48-55), and the blocking join runs on the main thread, not a runtime worker. The residual is the familiar remembered-order one, and materialized_runtime.rs exists precisely to write that order down.

title: Dropping `EvidenceRetention` while any reservation is alive blocks forever on the writer join

notes: Undecided inside its packet; needs crate::exchange_state / request_stages and the http-profile verifier — whether an exchange with no verifier-checked REQUEST_LABEL member can reach `Retention::reserve`.

adjudication.rationale: An unsigned request cannot reach `Retention::reserve`. Verification is the first stage of `handle` (http_profile_serve/mod.rs:450) and `floor_request` requires a `signature-input` header carrying a REQUEST_LABEL member plus a verifying signature over the rebuilt base (verify/floor/request.rs:83-115); `Retention::reserve` is only called from `commit_to_dispatch`, far downstream. So `component_list_for` never returns `None` for REQUEST_LABEL on the retention path, and the covered set always contains at least `content-digest` and `content-type` (mcp-re-http-profile/src/ids.rs:103-104). Independently, even an empty covered set would not collapse the key: `covered_headers` keeps `signature` and `signature-input` unconditionally (covered_set.rs:45-47), so the digest input always carries the per-request nonce, validity window, keyid and signature bytes. Two principals issuing the same method/target/body produce different digests.

title: The digest that keys every marker collapses to method+target+body for an unsigned request

adjudication.rationale: Same defect stated in R-SEAL terms: `complete` (durability.rs:331-350) binds the hop it writes to the commitment it discharges by nothing but the caller's discipline. Adjudicated as confirmed under 2f1deab67448a758, whose fix — `DispatchCommitted` carrying the retained request it committed to — removes the parameter entirely.

title: `complete` never binds the hop it writes to the commitment it discharges

adjudication.rationale: Confirmed as a classification defect, at lower severity than filed. `submit`'s `Err(_) => RetentionError::Store(BrokenPipe, 'retention writer stopped before acknowledging the write')` (durability.rs:214-218) is the only arm for a dropped acknowledgement, and `Store` is defined as 'nothing was published: the store is where it was' (transparency/mod.rs:135-136, :144-150) and answered 503 retry-safe by the serving path's catch-all (http_profile_serve/retention.rs:150-156). For a `Commit` job the rename at durable_writer.rs:99 can already have happened before the ack at :85 is lost, so a committed-stage marker — the artefact that reads as a crossed execution threshold — can survive an exchange the client is told to retry freely. That is the exact conflation `Unresolved` exists for (transparency/mod.rs:141-151) and that the memory rule 'never collapse execution certainty' forbids. Severity lowered from medium to low on reachability: `run_batch` unconditionally sends every ack (durable_writer.rs:76-86) and a closed channel is already caught as `StoreRetired` at try_send (durability.rs:202-208), so the window needs the writer thread to die holding a batch.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In `EvidenceRetention::submit`, resolve a lost acknowledgement by the job's DISPOSITION rather than as an ordinary outage: a pre-dispatch job (`PublishOrWithdraw`, `Commit`) whose ack never arrived may have left execution-signifying state, so it belongs in `RetentionError::Unresolved`; a post-dispatch `Publish` is already answered indeterminate by the caller either way. `submit` takes the `JobKind` it is about to send, so the distinction is available at the point the error is built.

title: The documented 2K queue argument omits the rescind job

adjudication.rationale: Already fixed in merged ancestry, at current HEAD. d009cccd ('security: tell a client the difference between a full queue and a dead writer', #895) closes this row by name — its message carries the heading 'R11-739: the unit's own argument was measured by nothing'. `proxy.retention_commitment`'s `tested_symbols` now names both capacity controls, with a comment giving the same reason the finding does: `lib#transparency::durability::tests::completion_is_never_refused_for_capacity` and `...::a_full_reservation_queue_is_refused_at_reserve_and_the_slot_returns` (verification/policy/verification.toml:3583-3587), and the unit now declares `mutation://` so probe M138 is not decoration (verification.toml:3540-3544). title: The unit closure adds `durability_bounds.rs` for the capacity argument but its battery names no capacity test

adjudication.rationale: The documented argument is wrong, and the reviewer is right that the rescind is what it omits — but the conclusion it supports still holds, so this is a claim defect rather than an unsound bound. durability_bounds.rs:13-16 and durability.rs:14-16 both assert that 'a reservation contributes at most one queued job at any instant, so K reservations bound the queue at K jobs'. That is false as written: `commit_to_dispatch` drops its `ReservedBeforeDispatch` on the way out (durability.rs:316), whose `Drop` try_sends a `Rescind` (reserved_before_dispatch.rs:115-123) that is never awaited, so the same reservation's completion job is enqueued alongside it — two jobs, one permit, no cancellation needed. Counting the true census: every other job a reservation sends is awaited, and because the writer is FIFO an ack proves every earlier job was drained, so at most one un-awaited rescind plus one awaited job can be outstanding per permit. That lands on 2K exactly — the number is right, the stated derivation (a permit-handover window) names the wrong second occupant, and the margin it implies is zero rather than one slot. Severity lowered from high: the bound is not violated by this mechanism (see the adjudication of eadcbe08 for what does violate it).
adjudication.smallest_fix: Restate the census in durability_bounds.rs exhaustively — per permit: one awaited job at a time (reserve, then commit, then complete) plus at most one un-awaited Drop-borne rescind, with the FIFO ack acting as the flush that keeps it at one — and say that 2K is therefore exactly tight rather than one slot of slack. The same false sentence is repeated in durability.rs:14-16 and must be corrected with it.

title: The write-queue capacity argument omits the Drop-borne rescind job, so "complete is never refused for capacity" is not established at 2K

notes: Undecided inside its packet; needs the per-core in-flight admission ceiling (named in durability_bounds.rs:12 as the primary control) — it may bound concurrency well below 1024

adjudication.rationale: The outside control the finding asked about is a BYTE budget, not a count, and it is what bounds this. `BodyByteBudget` caps resident request-body bytes per core at `max_body_bytes * BUFFERED_BODY_BUDGET_MULTIPLE` = 4 x 16 MiB = 64 MiB by default (async_serve/body_budget.rs:30-46, async_serve/core_admission.rs:66-72, tls.rs:139-143), charged as the body arrives and never from a declared length; and the guard is held for the WHOLE request — `_body_charge` at async_serve/request.rs:91 outlives `handler(...).await` at :129, so it is still held while the `JobKind::Publish` sits in the queue awaiting its ack (durability.rs:267-275). 1024 concurrent max-size completions would therefore require ~16 GiB of concurrently resident request bodies, refused at 64 MiB per core long before. The realistic ceiling on queued payload is roughly `cores x 64 MiB x 4/3` plus the response half — bounded and proportional to an operator-set limit. G11's factor-of-two is a CAPACITY argument ('complete is never refused for capacity', durability_bounds.rs:19-27) and claims nothing about memory, so nothing is broken. Residual worth one doc line: durability_bounds.rs:12 names 'the per-core in-flight ceiling' as the primary control when the byte budget is the one that bounds memory.

title: The write queue bounds job COUNT, not bytes: 1024 in-flight completions hold ~44 GB of record payload

adjudication.rationale: The conclusion is right and the mechanism is not. The Drop-borne rescind alone does not break the bound: it makes it exactly tight (one un-awaited rescind + one awaited job per permit = 2K, and a sync_channel of 2K accepts the 2K-th send). What actually breaks it is that the permit — the thing the whole argument counts — is released by a CANCELLED request future while that future's job is still in the queue. `reserve` holds the permit in a local (durability.rs:260-277): drop the future at the await and the permit returns while the job stays queued and un-acked. Same for `commit_to_dispatch` (durability.rs:306-317, which also queues the reservation's rescind on the way out) and for `complete`, whose job is orphaned while the caller still holds the permit-bearing `DispatchCommitted`. So a permit slot can account for three or more queued jobs, and repeated cancelled `reserve` attempts orphan a job each while handing the permit straight back — the queue can then fill to 2K with no bound from K at all, and `complete`'s `try_send` returns `Full` after the backend has run. Cancellation is reachable: hyper drops in-flight service futures when its connection future is dropped (async_serve/connection.rs:84-108). Severity medium, not high: the outcome is a 500 `EvidenceRetentionIndeterminate` with the `.pending` marker surviving (http_profile_serve/retention.rs:185-197), i.e. over-reported indeterminacy, not lost evidence, and it needs the writer thread to be thousands of jobs behind.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Make the permit outlive the job it admitted: have `WriteJob` carry the `Arc<AdmissionPermit>` (durable_job.rs:20-28), so a cancelled future cannot return a slot while its job is still queued and 'K permits bound the queue' becomes true of every job rather than of every job whose future ran to completion. Raising the capacity number instead would not fix it — repeated cancelled `reserve` attempts orphan jobs at a rate K does not bound.

notes: [att-batch74-001 senior] A lost or crash-resurrected marker-clear leaves a .pending over a landed hop: over-reported indeterminacy, the direction JobKind::Publish documents as safe post-dispatch; the token is decidable from stored bytes (it is EvidenceDigest of serde_json(RetainedRequest), and the hop record carries that s…

adjudication.rationale: The consequence is right and 'unreconcilable' is too strong. The link exists and is stated: the marker is named by `EvidenceDigest::of(serde_json::to_vec(&retained_request(request)))` (durability.rs:266-270) and the hop embeds that same `retained_request` value as its `request` field (retained_record.rs:88-99, :124-131), which `ReservationMarker` documents explicitly — 'the same token the marker is named by, and the same one a completed hop's request half hashes to' (reservation_marker.rs:38-41). So a stale `.pending` token CAN be matched to the hop that discharged it. What is missing is the projection: `RetainedHopRecord`, `RetainedRequest` and `retained_request` are all `pub(super)`, `RetainedArchive` exposes only `load`/`load_chain`/`object_path` (retained_archive.rs:84-110), and `RetainedHop` hands back a decoded `HttpRequest` — so an auditor would have to re-implement a private serde shape byte-for-byte to perform the reconciliation the marker exists for. The failure path itself is correct and deliberate: clearing the marker is best-effort and prints both paths (durable_writer.rs:158-181).
adjudication.smallest_fix: Expose the derivation that already exists: a `request_digest` projection on `RetainedArchive` (or on the loaded hop) computed from `retained_request`, so `pending_reservations()` tokens can be matched against retained hops through the read surface instead of by replicating a `pub(super)` serde shape. No new fact is stored and the marker's content is unchanged.

adjudication.rationale: The code facts hold, but the reviewer's harm story does not: nothing 'reports it as installed'. `build_revocation_resolver` builds the Live tier with `LiveTrustResolver::new(base)` (revocation_resolver.rs:63-65), so `revocation` is `None` on every production path; `with_revocation_source` (live_trust.rs:85-94) and `resolve_with_revocation_id` (:103-131) are `pub(super)` with `#[allow(dead_code)]` and only this file's tests call them; the field doc says NOT WIRED (:58-69) and the trait impl's own doc says the second authority 'is reached only through the inherent method' (:134-139). So every sentence in the file is accurate and no invalid value exists today. What is real is structural: one representation carries two resolution surfaces with different security semantics, and the only surface the composition root can reach — `dyn TrustResolver` — is the weaker one. Possession of a `LiveTrustResolver` holding `Some(revocation)` does not mean revocation is enforced; which it means depends on which method the caller picked. That is the shape this repo already handled by TYPE one module over: `window_policy::ApplicableClassWindows` exists precisely so the compiler records which input is missing rather than a comment saying so (window_policy.rs:80-102). Here the same dormancy is carried by prose and an attribute.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Make the missing input structural rather than documented, the way `ApplicableClassWindows` does: the input this seam lacks is a `revocation_id` on the `TrustResolver` trait, so a `LiveTrustResolver` that holds a source should not be obtainable as a `dyn TrustResolver` at all — e.g. move the source-bearing form behind its own type whose only resolution entry point is `resolve_with_revocation_id`, leaving `LiveTrustResolver` with no `revocation` field to ignore. Do NOT delete the seam: the ADR-MCPS-013 elaboration is a record the tree deliberately keeps.

CROSS-CONNECTION STARVATION UNDER EXHAUSTION: ACCEPTED RISK (availability, not integrity/confidentiality). The budget protects the signing backend's GLOBAL capacity, shared with delegated-key issuance; TLS 1.3 signs before client authentication, the signer receives no connection identity and a connection signs at most once, so the only available discriminator is source address, which the owner declined as a security boundary (bypassable by distributed sources and IPv6 churn, unfair behind NAT, a second resource policy without principal isolation). Sufficient concurrent or adversarial handshake demand can exhaust the budget and refuse legitimate handshakes until it refills; exhaustion fails closed (no fallback signer, no path around the bucket). No per-peer isolation is claimed. A future design may revisit fairness only if a trustworthy principal or connection identity exists before the signing decision. HandshakeQuotaWindow (handshake_quota.rs) is a distinct, non-configurable reactive mechanism over the same quota (refuse locally for one network-timeout window after a provider throttle); not a duplicate policy.
title: The delegated TLS handshake-signature budget is one listener-wide bucket with no per-peer dimension and no operator knob, so unauthenticated ClientHello volume can starve legitimate full handshakes

adjudication.rationale: The `.ok()?` on the `high_water` mutex is real (signing_plane/mod.rs:275), but the failure mode built on it cannot occur, for two independent reasons. First, `DelegatedEpochWatch` is never shared: it is built in `materialize` and MOVED whole into the rotation worker's closure (signing_plane/mod.rs:198-204; rotation.rs:41-49), so the only thread that can ever hold the guard is the rotation thread itself. Second, the only way that thread can poison the mutex is to panic inside `current_label`'s critical section — a comparison, a store and a `format!` — and `supervise_delegated_rotation` (rotation.rs:75-93) wraps the ENTIRE `rotation_loop` in `catch_unwind` and converts any panic into `signer.retire_permanently()` plus `metrics().record_failure()` and a FATAL log, after which the thread returns and the loop does not run again. A grep for `catch_unwind` across mcp-re-proxy/src confirms there is no other handler anywhere on this path, so the described steady state — poisoned mark, `None` forever, rotor recording failures and backing off to the 30s ceiling while the current key serves to its `exp` — is unreachable: the panic that would create it already retired the signer permanently and killed the loop. The remaining claim, that two locks in one owner encode different poison policies, is true but stylistic; the neighbouring `RwLock` recovers because it IS shared across the fleet and read on every request (mod.rs:109-116), which this mutex is not.

adjudication.rationale: Verified in both tiers. `ContinuationPlane::wired` (continuation/mod.rs:79-87) takes a bare `i64` and validates nothing, and it is reached from the `pub`, crate-external `HttpProfileProxy::with_continuation_store` (http_profile_serve/mod.rs:349-356). adjudication.rationale: The attack chain checks out against the real dispatcher. The loop then refuses to mint at all and backs off (trust_epoch_advance.rs:81-83,95-116). Each replica serves its current key to exp, at most ttl later, and then fails closed. Recovery needs the counter restored to or above every replica's high-water mark, or a fleet restart. The module doc now states the dependency for the advance direction (signing_plane/mod.rs:227-229), but nothing bounds or alarms on it beyond eprintln and the unconsumed metrics. c3600dad: FIXED (owner ruling 27.2, batch B-EPOCH). Regression: DelegatedEpochWatch (signing_plane/epoch_watch.rs) still refuses a read below its in-process high-water mark H, never lowers H, and on that refusal (or an absent counter once H is held) moves the shared key past H (amended below) and errors on a non-integer; concurrent repairs converge on max(H), an INCR above H is never overwritten, minting resumes on the next read >= H. A replica with no H writes nothing. Each refusal prints its state (REGRESSED / unreadable / repair FAILED naming the GET/SET/EVAL access needed). Advance: the counter is the operator's revocation action; whoever may write it holds that authority by design (module doc, fleet guide prerequisites: rediss + credentials). Repair target amended in 4372a575 (see below). Controls: epoch_watch::tests (7), trust_epoch::raise::tests (1), probes M500 (no repair) and M501 (raise to the regressed read) red, M447/M448 re-anchored and red; live suites trust_epoch::raise::live (3) and epoch_watch::live (1) passed against Redis 7 locally and run in live-infra-e2e.yml. 4372a575: the repair writes H+1 (checked_add; refused without a write at i64::MAX) via EpochRaiser::raise_past(H, H+1), one EVAL that SETs only while the counter is absent or below H, so a rollback acts as a forward rotation: the repairing replica never re-enters its pre-rollback label and an INCR against the rolled-back store that leaves it below H ends past H. Not closed by the repair and stated in signing_plane/epoch_watch.rs and the fleet guide: replicas with different marks are not ordered (a repair from a lower mark can equal a higher replica's mark, which then keeps its pre-rollback label; test a_repair_from_a_lower_mark_can_land_on_a_higher_replicas_label), and an INCR that brings the rolled-back key back to exactly the mark before any read is indistinguishable from no rollback. Probe M502 (repair to H) red.

notes: Undecided inside its packet; needs crate::transparency::EvidenceRetention — whether an uncompleted `DispatchCommitted` is a recognised terminal state of the record, or an anomaly.

adjudication.rationale: The factual claim verifies exactly: `retention.complete` has one call site, `retain_accepted` (mcp-re-proxy/src/http_profile_serve/reply_assembly/accepted.rs:111-117), which is reached from only two places — `serve_retained` (accepted.rs:47) and `answer_notification`'s Ok arm (notification.rs:60) — so every post-crossing refusal (`assemble_reply`'s four arms at reply_assembly/mod.rs:98, 107, 111, 78; notification.rs:89; notification.rs:122) returns without discharging it. The out-of-packet question is answered half in the design's favour: an uncompleted `DispatchCommitted` is a RECOGNISED state, not an anomaly — the `.pending` marker means 'this request crossed the execution threshold and its outcome was never retained', it deliberately has no `Drop`, and over-reporting indeterminacy is stated as the safe direction (mcp-re-proxy/src/transparency/dispatch_committed.rs:21-36). What survives is a real evidence loss on a reachable path: with retention on, a backend reply with an unrecognized `resultType` yields a signed 502 at mcp-re-proxy/src/http_profile_serve/reply.rs:97, the client receives bytes the deployment then retains nothing about, and the module's own claim that a retention deployment 'can account for everything it served' (retention.rs:4-5) fails for that class. The marker left behind is also unreachable operationally: `pending_reservations()` (transparency/durability.rs:292-294) has zero production callers — its only caller is a test — so nothing enumerates or reaps them and they accumulate one file per forced refusal.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Route post-crossing refusals through the same discharge the success terminals use: the refusal response IS the served response, so `retain_accepted` (which already returns `Some(rejection)` on its own failure) should be called with it before the refusal is returned. That turns the `.pending` marker into a completed hop naming the actual outcome, and reserves genuine indeterminacy for the case it was designed for — a process that died mid-exchange.

adjudication.rationale: The ordering is as described and the consequence is not. `apply_pending_invalidations` does `self.channel.drain_pending()` first (push_trust.rs:80) and `TrustEpochSource::drain_pending` is a `std::mem::take` (trust_epoch.rs:191-193), so a drained event is gone. But the ONLY way the subsequent apply fails is a poisoned cache mutex — `evict` returns false (trust_cache.rs:333-335) and `clear` returns 0 (:368-370) on `Err` from `self.cache.lock()` — and in exactly that state `cached` returns `Some(Err(Unavailable))` for EVERY lookup, unconditionally and before any entry is consulted (:235-243), so `BoundedTrustCache::resolve` returns at step 1 (:390-392) and serves nothing at all. `std::sync::Mutex` poisoning is permanent and this type never calls `into_inner`, so the refusal is total and the lost flush changes nothing a request can observe. The multi-thread window the finding also names — one core drains a FlushAll while another serves a hit before `clear()` lands — is the duration of one mutex acquisition plus a `retain`, against a stated bound of one poll interval (5s, trust_plane/mod.rs:360), so it is inside the noise of the guarantee rather than a violation of it. One real inaccuracy nearby, recorded on R11-734 instead: `clear`'s doc says a poisoned lock leaves 'the bounded-T fallback' capping the window, when in fact nothing is served at all.

adjudication.rationale: Confirmed, with the exploit bound tightened. The record is unauthenticated end to end: `encode` produces `<generation>:<status>` (redis_admission_source.rs:41-48), `publish` is a bare `SET` (:117-121), `current_state` a bare `GET` (:152-155), and `decode` accepts any well-formed pair (:66-78) with no signature, MAC, CAS or monotonicity check. `AuthoritativeAdmission::new` accepts any `u64` generation, and the R-SEAL test has nothing to delete because there is no check. The premise gap is real at current main: enumerating verification/policy/assumptions.toml shows NO assumption covering admission-store write authority (the only shared-store premises are ASM-0040/0041 for replay and ASM-0044 for the trust epoch), and THM-0004's scope explicitly disclaims it (verification/policy/theorems.toml:289-291). Reachable failure: an actor with write access to the instance — a co-tenant, a leaked credential, a compromised sidecar — issues `SET mcp-re:admission:<victim> 5:admitted`, and check_admission's currency arm (mcp-re-http-profile/src/admission.rs:443-461) accepts it as the authority's word. BOUND (from R11-506, and verified): the writer cannot admit an arbitrary workload, because the call must still carry an authority-signed assertion for the presenting actor at that same generation (admission.rs:406-441) and within N + skew (admission.rs:264-329). What a writer CAN do is reverse any revocation, or rewind a generation so a retained older assertion becomes current — for as long as the revoked workload holds an unexpired assertion. That bounded-but-total defeat of the revocation channel is why this is high rather than critical.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Cheapest closure that changes the security argument: register an ASM in verification/policy/assumptions.toml naming who may write `mcp-re:admission:*` (scoped to the admission unit and boundary.shared_state_store, with an owner and a review requirement), exactly as ASM-0040 does for the replay tier — the record's provenance then stops being an unstated premise. The structural fix is to have the authority sign `<admission_id>:<generation>:<status>` under the same root the assertions are signed under and have `decode` refuse an unverifiable record as a definitive negative (never as an outage), plus a CAS on publish so a generation can only advance.

(claims.rs:123-126) — since `iss` makes no refusal possible.

A redis-wait-quorum tier's quorum and timeout_ms are bounded below (>= 1) but not above in both the parser and the layer-A state guard, so an operator value such as redis-wait-quorum:4294967295:<huge> classifies as a legal SharedRedis state and sizes the Redis client response deadline (timeout_ms + 2s) and the WAIT timeout to effectively unbounded, turning a fail-closed refusal into an indefinite admission hang. Every request reaches this guard (classify -> wait_quorum_guards), parser or in-process. Control: config_state::replay::tests::a_wait_quorum_timeout_past_the_ceiling_names_no_state_and_the_ceiling_does (one past refused, ceiling accepted unchanged); probe M526 red. Quorum needs no ceiling: WAIT returns at timeout_ms whatever the quorum, so a quorum the deployment cannot meet refuses every admission fail-closed and bounded by the timeout ceiling; it cannot lengthen the await. Documented in docs/sidecar-deployment-guide.md.

adjudication.rationale: The mechanism holds exactly as described. `Clone for InMemoryReplayCache` on a poisoned source returns `max_entries: 0` with `seen: Mutex::new(BTreeMap::new())` — a fresh, unpoisoned mutex over an EMPTY map (mcp-re-core/src/replay.rs:270-277). The only thing that then refuses is `seen.len() >= self.max_entries` with both at 0 (replay.rs:371). `pub fn with_max_entries(mut self, max_entries: usize) -> Self` (replay.rs:309-312) takes `self` by value and overwrites the field on any inhabitant, so `poisoned.clone().with_max_entries(1_000)` is a fully functional cache holding none of the source's admitted nonces and reporting no error, while `a_clone_of_a_poisoned_cache_admits_nothing` (replay.rs:596) keeps passing. This is R-SEAL's shape: the safety property is a field value a public builder can set back, and the unsafe state (empty AND admitting) is a legal, indistinguishable inhabitant. Reachability is indirect — it needs an embedder that clones a poisoned cache and then resizes it — and the proxy keeps this cache off the serving path via `is_single_process_reference`, so low rather than the reviewer's implicit higher reading.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In `mcp-re-core/src/replay.rs`, represent the unreadable-source state structurally instead of numerically: a private field (or an enum over the seen-set) that `check_and_insert` refuses on regardless of `max_entries`, set by `Clone`'s poisoned arm and untouched by `with_max_entries`. Then a poisoned clone refuses whatever a later builder call says.

title: A clone of a poisoned cache is safe only because `max_entries` stays 0, and `with_max_entries` is public

adjudication.rationale: The smell is real; the fix site the reviewer names is theatre. `ReplayKey`'s five fields are `pub` with no constructor (mcp-re-core/src/replay.rs:111-131) and the tier charges `key.principal` verbatim (async_replay/mod.rs:210, 224) while keying on `key.signer/audience/nonce` (mod.rs:201). But `ReplayKey` lives in `mcp-re-core` and its ONLY production producer is `HttpReplayKey::to_core_replay_key` in a DIFFERENT crate (mcp-re-http-profile/src/replay.rs:113-121; the sole consumer is http_profile_dispatch.rs:165). Module privacy in `mcp-re-core` therefore cannot reach that producer: it would force a public constructor taking the same five strings with the same absence of checking, and core cannot perform the derivation because the keyid boundary is a profile fact and core is deliberately profile-agnostic and pure (replay.rs:103-110). That is exactly the case CLAUDE.md calls privacy theatre. The invariant's real owner is one field higher up: `HttpReplayKey.actor_id` is a raw `String` (http-profile/src/replay.rs:41), and both invariants this owner rests on are functions of it — `principal_slot`'s `rsplit_once(':')` lands on the keyid boundary only because `ActorIdentity::field_escape` escapes ':' (block.rs:87-96), and `signer_slot`'s U+001F join is injective only because the same function escapes U+001F. The other four components are a compile-time constant (`PROFILE_TAG`, verify/floor/request.rs:136), a constant label, a base64url hash, and a slot that `composite_replay_key` length-prefixes anyway (shared_replay.rs:115-126). So exactly one component is unowned, and it is the one all the reasoning depends on. Note #885 (97e6b8db) already added `the_principal_slot_is_the_subject_without_its_keyid` and the injectivity control, so the derivation is test-owned even though it is not type-owned — severity revised from medium to low.

That makes the keyid boundary and the separator-freedom properties of every inhabitant instead of properties of `prepare_http_dispatch`. Do NOT touch `mcp-re-core::ReplayKey`: privatising it there only relocates the same unchecked five arguments.

A peer therefore cannot mint principals; it can only present under kids the operator enrolled, and the keyid is deliberately dropped so extra keys do not multiply one subject. Driving the budget to 1 requires ~800,000 distinct enrolled subjects holding entries simultaneously AND the tier already past the pressure line (`under_pressure` needs `held >= max_entries - max_entries/5 = 800_000`, mcp-re-proxy/src/async_replay/bounds.rs:81-83). adjudication.rationale: Confirmed at rotation.rs:166-182. The steady-state wait polls the shared epoch roughly every 500 ms but breaks out only on `matches!(watch.current_label(), Some(l) if l != last_label)` (line 173), so a `None` — the unreadable-store or regressed-counter case, which `DelegatedEpochWatch::current_label` returns at signing_plane/mod.rs:274-280 — is indistinguishable from `unchanged` and the loop keeps sleeping until `exp - overlap`. Only when the window opens does `observe_trust_epoch` see the `None` and route to `refuse_to_mint_without_a_comparable_epoch` (trust_epoch_advance.rs:58-59), which is the first thing that calls `record_failure` (trust_epoch_advance.rs:77). With the default TTL 300 / overlap 60 that is up to 240 s during which `consecutive_failures` reads 0 while the operator's cross-fleet kill switch has been unreadable. Fail-quiet, not fail-open: the replica correctly keeps serving and correctly refuses to mint later. The reason to fix it is the module's own precedent — rotation.rs:62-68 argues that `consecutive_failures` is written only by this thread, so a surface that keeps reading 0 while nothing is working is exactly the failure the supervisor was added to remove.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In `wait_for_window` (mcp-re-proxy/src/signing_plane/rotation.rs:170-177) distinguish the three answers instead of two: on the first `None` observed during the wait, record a failure on the signer's metrics (and break out so `observe_trust_epoch` states the refusal), rather than treating an unreadable counter as `unchanged` until the schedule next happens to look.

adjudication.rationale: The outside source disproves the failure story. The composition root reads the classified authorization state and the evaluator from ONE consuming `into_parts()` — `capability::evaluator(config.state().authorization(), .., &values.audience, ..)` at app.rs:544-551 — and `Established::on`/`off` is what decides both halves together, so there is no path on which the posture line says PDP-DECISION and the artifact is absent (capability.rs:45, :88-92; the file's doc at capability.rs:33-36 and app.rs:539-543 state that pairing). A `--authz pdp-decision` deployment that enrols no `authorization-issuer` key is a startup REFUSAL (capability.rs:50-58), not a silent default. `HttpProfileProxy::new` (http_profile_serve/mod.rs:280) is the only place the default stage is used and `with_authorization` (mod.rs:340-341) is unconditionally applied at app.rs:806-808 whenever an evaluator exists; app.rs is the only production composition root. `AuthzKind` is a closed three-variant enum, so there is no unrecognised kind to fall through. Residual (not a defect): `#[derive(Default)]` on serving.rs:34 is a robustness preference — the finding itself states there is no attacker story.

title: The fail-closed `exp` bound is a property of call ordering, not of the value that holds the key

adjudication.rationale: The premise that makes this a defect — that an exchange can outlive its snapshot's `exp` and still sign under it — does not hold, because `now` is fixed for the whole exchange and is never re-read. `Exchange::now` is set once in `handle` (http_profile_serve/mod.rs:459-465) and documented as fixed at mod.rs:158-161 and 168-174. The snapshot on the exchange is produced ONLY by `answerable_stage` via `self.responses.window(ex.now)` -> `SigningWindow::open(&self.signer, now, ...)` -> `signer.current(now)`, which is exactly where `now < exp` is enforced (answering_commitment.rs:73-87 and 168; receipt/mod.rs:68-70; signing_window.rs:41-45; delegated_server_signer/mod.rs:213-216). Every refusal then calls `signed_rejection` with `ex.now` — the SAME instant — (receipt/mod.rs:118-153, receipt/audit_event.rs:62-70 and 104-112), and `signed_rejection` passes that same `now` into `SigningWindow::over` (receipt/artifact.rs:64-66). So `over`'s credential always satisfies `now < exp` on the production path, whatever the exchange's wall-clock duration, and a stalled backend or slow-read client changes nothing. `over` exists precisely so that a signer RETIRED between ANSWERABLE and a post-dispatch refusal does not degrade the one receipt that must state the backend may have acted into an unsigned body (artifact.rs:34-40, answering_commitment.rs:11-13, mod.rs:167-174); making it fallible on `now < exp` would reintroduce that defect for no gain. G2/THM-0063 are also honest as written: they claim the advertised validity is `min(now + ttl, exp)`, which `over` does own (signing_window.rs:52-60), and the module doc says `validity`, not `usability`. The residual R-SEAL point — that `over`'s caller, not the type, carries `now < exp` — is real but unreachable, and its only current exploit path is the test at request_stages.rs:256.

notes: Undecided inside its packet; needs crate::delegated_server_signer (rotation cadence / credential TTL) and crate::async_inner (whether the dispatch is bounded by a per-request timeout short enough to make the window unreachable)

adjudication.rationale: The mechanism verifies and the harm is reachable, though by a different route than the finding names. `answerable_stage` validates the credential at `ex.now` only (mcp-re-proxy/src/http_profile_serve/answering_commitment.rs:77, via `current(now)`'s `now < a.exp` at delegated_server_signer/mod.rs:214), the snapshot is carried across the backend round trip and signs both the reply and every later refusal receipt with `created = ex.now` and `expires = min(ex.now + sig_ttl, key.exp)` (receipt/mod.rs:97-111; signing_window.rs:52-59; artifact.rs:64-66). Nothing re-reads the wall clock, so the response's whole RFC 9421 freshness window is consumed by dispatch latency. The client's floor verifier refuses when `expires + skew <= now` (mcp-re-http-profile/src/verify/floor/params.rs:80-85). Concrete reachable failure: `sig_ttl_secs` is hard-coded to 300 at app.rs:725 and the default skew is 30 (VerifierPolicy::DEFAULT_MAX_CLOCK_SKEW, mcp-re-http-profile/src/policy.rs:108), while the inner-plane timeout is operator-set from `--read-timeout-secs` (app.rs:685-689). An operator who raises it past ~330s for long-running tool calls makes EVERY receipt for a call that outlasts the window fail the client's freshness check for a call that executed — the at-least-once hazard the ANSWERABLE stage exists to remove, relocated to 'stale at signing'. The second, narrower route is the one the finding describes: during a root-issuance outage the active credential runs down inside its 60s overlap (custody/issuance_terms.rs:36-38; overlap default 60, TTL 300), so `expires = key.exp` can be seconds away and any dispatch longer than that plus skew produces the same refusal. The ADR-MCPRE-052 §4 obligation quoted at signing_window.rs:4-8 is enforced against the frozen parameter, not against real time.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Make the credential's liveness a property of the window at the instant it is used: give `SigningWindow::over` a fallible form that refuses when `now >= key.exp` (which also closes R11-482), and base `created`/`expires` on a wall clock read at the signing boundary rather than on `ex.now`, refusing — not degrading to an unsigned error — when the credential has closed. A deployment-level complement: refuse at ANSWERABLE any credential whose remaining life is shorter than the inner-plane dispatch deadline plus skew, so the window cannot be outlived by the round trip it must cover.

notes: [att-batch39-002 senior] Rust cannot enumerate a data-carrying enum's variants without a derive or a mirror enum, so no in-file construction forces the vec entry; the witness match sits beside the list in one hunk, and the security property per form is also pinned by named tests.

adjudication.rationale: Exactly as read. `every_form()` builds `forms` as a four-element literal (config_state/transport.rs:472-482) and then runs a `for form in &forms { match form { ...four arms... => {} } }` (transport.rs:483-491). Adding a fifth `PeerIdentityEvidenceRequest` variant makes that match non-exhaustive and breaks the build, but the author closes the build by adding an ARM and nothing then requires an entry in the vec — so the doc at transport.rs:470-471 ('a form added to the union stops this list compiling, so no test below can enumerate a stale variant set') is half true: it stops the FILE compiling, not the list going stale. The two tests that read as exhaustive over the union, `the_identity_field_names_the_state_and_the_form_decides_whether_there_is_one` (transport.rs:497-520) and `only_exact_binding_becomes_a_state_and_every_other_kind_is_refused_aloud` (transport.rs:526-542), would silently stop covering the new form. I overturn the suggested fix: 'derive the list from a match that RETURNS a form per variant' does not close it on its own, because there is no discriminant value to match over — the witness has to observe the constructed set.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Make the witness observe the CONSTRUCTED set in `every_form()` (config_state/transport.rs:472-492): match each element into a per-variant covered-flags array and assert every flag is set. A fifth variant then forces both a fifth arm (compile) and a fifth flag that stays false (test failure) until an entry is added to `forms`.

adjudication.rationale: The visibility reading is right — `pub enum ChannelBindingState { ExactUriSan, ExactDnsSan }` (config_state/transport.rs:42-48) is re-exported at config_state/mod.rs:98 out of a `pub mod config_state` (lib.rs:55), so both variants are public constructors in and outside the crate. But R-SEAL does not bite here and the finding's own operational test says so: the type has NO illegal inhabitant (both variants are legal deployable postures), so 'illegal local state cannot be publicly constructed' is vacuous, and there is no check to delete — removing the `CnLegacy` refusal at transport.rs:144-151 still yields `None`, because no `ChannelBindingState` names a CN. The sibling contrast is not like-for-like: `CrlRevocationState` (transport.rs:55-63) seals DATA — a path list and a cadence whose COMBINATIONS CF-04 refuses — and there is no analogous data here. What the contract asserts that the type cannot carry is provenance: 'Holding `Some(state)` is the proof that the deployment NAMED the one deployable binding form' is an origin claim over a fieldless `Copy` enum, precisely the form that cannot survive a copy. The production path is sound: `classify_binding` (transport.rs:135-160) is the only production producer and app.rs:559 the only production consumer.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Narrow the contract text rather than the type: `ChannelBindingState` ENUMERATES the two deployable postures (it has no illegal inhabitant), `classify_binding` (config_state/transport.rs:135-160) is its sole production producer and app.rs:559 its sole production consumer. adjudication.rationale: The facts hold and the plane is genuinely inconsistent with itself. `cached` maps a poisoned cache mutex to `Some(Err(Unavailable))` (trust_cache.rs:235-243), `std::sync::Mutex` poisoning is permanent and `BoundedTrustCache` never calls `into_inner`, so one panic while the lock is held turns every subsequent verification on that replica into `trust_resolver_unavailable` for the process lifetime, under both the bounded-cache and push tiers. The other two mutex owners in the same plane take the opposite position and say why: `trust_epoch::recover` recovers because 'treating poison as a failure instead drops an operator's revocation on the floor permanently and silently' (trust_epoch.rs:32-43), and `ReloadingTrustStore::snapshot` recovers because 'the request path must not panic because a writer paniced mid-swap' (reloading_trust.rs:113-121). Three owners, three policies, none stated as the plane's. The direction here is fail-closed and the guarded region only does HashMap operations and a `VerificationKey` clone, so it is a latent availability cliff rather than a trust hole. One concrete inaccuracy to fix with it: `clear`'s doc claims a poisoned lock leaves 'the bounded-T fallback still capping the exposure window' (:364-365) and `evict`'s says 'the next read fails closed via `cached`' (:328-329) — the second is right and the first is not, because in that state nothing is served at all.
adjudication.smallest_fix: State the trust plane's poisoning policy once, in `trust_cache`'s module doc, and make this type agree with it: the data behind the lock is a cache and is safe to read after a panic, so recover the guard the way `trust_epoch::recover` does rather than latching a permanent refusal no surface reports. Correct `clear`'s doc in the same change — a poisoned lock does not leave the bounded-T fallback capping anything.

adjudication.rationale: Verified, and the workspace sharpens it. `system_clock` reads `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)` (trust_cache.rs:65-69); every deadline is an absolute Unix second (`expires_at` from `now.checked_add(ttl)`, :280) and every hit test is `now < entry.expires_at` (:248). A backward wall-clock step of d therefore extends every live entry by d, and `evict`/`clear`/the opportunistic prune read the same clock (:273, :332, :367). The module's own doc reasons about exactly this hazard in the OTHER direction and only there — an unrepresentable reading yields `i64::MAX` because 'the opposite clamp would place every entry written under a real clock permanently inside its window' (:60-64) — so the file documents a completeness it does not have. What makes this the cleanest term to fix: the other half of the delivered window is already monotonic. `Halt::sleep` bounds the reload cadence with `Instant` (managed_worker/halt.rs:60-78) and the epoch poller uses `thread::sleep` plus `Instant::elapsed` (trust_epoch.rs:115-125, :417-431), so of the two terms in the printed `R + T`, only `T` is measured on a clock an outside actor can move. Exposure is bounded by the size of the step and requires influence over host time (NTP step, VM snapshot restore, hypervisor sync), so this is lower than the reviewer's medium.
adjudication.smallest_fix: Inside `BoundedTrustCache`, make an entry's deadline a monotonic quantity (an `Instant`, or a monotonic-second reading injected the way `UnixClock` is) so `T` cannot be lengthened by a clock step, keeping the wall clock only for anything that must be comparable across processes — nothing in this type is. The injected-clock seam and the tighten-only ceiling logic stay as they are; only the source the deadline is measured against changes.

adjudication.rationale: Verified from source. `TrustDocument::parse` does `entries.iter().find(|e| e.key_id == key_id)` inside the per-entry loop (trust_document.rs:124), so the duplicate-key_id rule is O(n^2) string comparisons in the number of enrolments, and `VerificationKey::from_b64url` runs once per entry per parse (:139). `read_trust_file` re-parses the whole document on every reload cycle (trust_plane/snapshot.rs:41-45, called from `trust_reload_cycle` at reload/mod.rs:135), and the cadence can legally be 1s, so a large signer roster pays the full quadratic scan every second on the reload thread — which nothing supervises for latency (the supervisor at reload/supervision.rs:34 catches panics, not slowness). No attacker story: the file is operator-controlled and anyone who can grow it can already enrol signers. This is a scaling cliff with a trivial linear form, and the uniqueness rule is a set-membership fact, not a rescan. R11-729 (ledger 4c6f885fc3ab222f) mentions the same scan in passing, but its fix is filesystem posture plus a read size cap at a different owner, so this is not folded into it.
adjudication.smallest_fix: In `TrustDocument::parse`, carry a `HashMap<&str, &str>` (key_id -> prior signer) alongside `entries` so the uniqueness rule is one hash lookup rather than a linear rescan. adjudication.rationale: Correct as read. `add_key` is the only mutator of the trust map in either verifier — `self.keys.retain(|entry| entry.key_id != key_id); self.keys.push(...)` (v1.rs:180-184, v2.rs:438-442) — and `permit_ingress_identity` (v2.rs:446-449) only inserts into a `BTreeSet`. There is no `remove_key`, no expiry, and no operation over the SET, so `retain` covers only rotation that REUSES a key id; minting `attestor-2` and retiring `attestor-1` leaves `attestor-1` trusted for the process lifetime. The doc comment is not the defect — v1.rs:177-179 claims exactly the narrower same-id property — the SHAPE is: trust is accumulated per-value rather than being a projection of the configured set. Unreachable today (Modes B and C refused at config_state/transport.rs:184-191 and 287-298), and in fact there is no production constructor for either verifier at all, so this is the deferred half's own change rule applying (ingress/mod.rs:23-25: the suite is the only thing keeping it correct, and a check is not weakened because nothing reaches it).
adjudication.smallest_fix: Take the trust material at construction rather than accumulating it: `LbAssertionBinding::new(source, keys)` and `LbAssertionV2Binding::new(source, audience, keys, ingress_identities)`, with the `Vec<LbKeyEntry>` / `BTreeSet<String>` private and no `&mut self` mutator. 'Trusted' then means 'in the configured set', rotation is a new verifier, and the clone-divergence reported as R11-682 closes in the same edit.

Every v1 test builds its verifier through `binding_with_lb_key` (v1.rs:302-306) and every v2 test through `v2_binding` (v2.rs:606-614); each adds exactly one key, so nothing adds two keys under one id and both stated mutations survive green. Inverting `retain`'s predicate to `==` deletes every OTHER key; dropping the `retain` leaves two entries under one id and `key_for`'s `find` (v1.rs:187-192, v2.rs:452-457) returns the FIRST, so the RETIRED key keeps verifying — the exact failure the doc at v1.rs:177-179 and v2.rs:435-437 claims to prevent. The contract is honest (G19 is labelled code-reading-only), so this is an evidence gap rather than an over-claim — but ingress/mod.rs:23-25 makes this half's own suite the only thing keeping it correct, which is what turns a missing control here into a real finding.
adjudication.smallest_fix: One control per verifier, beside the existing key-lookup tests: add key A under id `lb-1` / `attestor-1`, then add key B under the SAME id, and require an assertion signed by A to fail `BadSignature` while one signed by B verifies. That kills both mutations — the inverted `retain` and the dropped `retain`.
